hints: Look closely at the very top edge of tissue X facing the lumen, can you see the tiny hair-like fringe and the paler cells dotted among the epithelium?
Tissue Y is the dark, wavy band of fibres just below X and above the cartilage, think which muscle type changes airway diameter during ventilation or an asthma attack.
walkthrough:
**Identify tissue X from its position**

Tissue X lines the lumen of the bronchus, so it is the lining epithelium. You can see a fuzzy border on top (cilia) with goblet cells underneath. This is ciliated epithelium with mucus-secreting goblet cells.

**Identify tissue Y from its position**

Tissue Y is the layer of fibres just below the epithelium and above the large cartilage plate at the bottom. Its wavy, spindle-shaped fibres are smooth muscle, not cartilage and not elastic fibres.

**Match each tissue to its job**

Cilia do not make mucus, they beat to waft mucus with trapped dust upwards toward the throat. Smooth muscle contracts to constrict (narrow) the airway and relaxes to allow dilation. That combination is option D.

options.A: X does contain goblet cells that secrete mucus, but the main visible function tested here is the cilia wafting. Y is smooth muscle, while preventing collapse is the job of the cartilage plate at the bottom.
options.B: Support comes from cartilage, not from X. Y can relax to help dilate, but its active contraction constricts the airway, so this pair is reversed.
options.C: Trapping is done by sticky mucus, not by X as a whole, and Y does not secrete mucus. Secretion is by goblet cells in the epithelium.
options.D: Well done. X is ciliated epithelium whose cilia waft dust-laden mucus upwards, and Y is smooth muscle whose contraction constricts the airway.
